FREE STATE HAEMORRHAGING HEALTHCARE (2016)

By: Este de Klerk | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Carte Blanche have been uncovering widespread maladministration in healthcare in the FS for the past three years. We go back to see if anything has changed.

Unique Selling Point:
The Free State Health department has been cash-strapped and under administration from the provincial legislature since 2014. They've had a debt of R700 million when they started the financial year in 2015/2016 - a debt, the department now says they have decreased to R200 million. A save of R500 million in just two financial years?
Coupled with this, 24% of the province's doctors have resigned between 2014 - 2015, with another 14 specialists leaving in 2016. This has put the School of Medicine at the University of the Free State at great risk in terms of its accreditation and students - undergraduate and post-graduate are saying that they are not getting adequate training.
Bongani Hospital in Welkom has lost its accreditation from the HPCSA this year and from the 1st of January 2017 the hospital will not be allowed to train and teach interns anymore.


Summary:
Our source at Bongani Hospital also claims that by the end of October there will only be one specialists left, and by the end of December only one. However, the department is denying this, saying Bongani Hospital has a full spectrum of specialists and the hospital is able to provide all the necessary health services.

The HOD of the FS department, dr David Motau, further says that healthcare in the province is at a healthy state and that they are improving. But this is not what doctors on the ground experience - doctors and nurses who have spoken to us in hidden identity. It is also not what human rights organisations, Section27 and the TAC are experiencing when they talk to medical practitioners on the ground.
Just last week there were strikes at the Monapo Hospital in Qwaqwa again.


Further information:
Our case studies tell horrendous stories of alleged medical malpractice that resulted in them losing their babies.
The Carte Blanche Paediatric High Care Ward at Universitas Hospital has been closed for the month of August - confirmed by the head of Paediatrics, but then denied by the HOD. We also asked him why, if it is in fact our ward, the department didn't want to give us permission to go and film there. The HOD said because we will film footage in a hospital and we are not allowed to, but that the department wants to ask Carte Blanche to please donate more equipment to the hospitals in the Free State.

The Minister of Health says the National Department is concerned about what is going on in the Free State province's healthcare.
But the Minister admitted that he cannot hire of fire any MEC for Health. He doesn't have the authority to do so. Only the Premier of a province can do that.
So, is change in the Free State healthcare really possible with a MEC for health and a HOD for health who both say healthcare in the province is not bad and in a healthy state? There have been consistent calls for MEC, dr Benny Malakoane's head for years.
There are several investigations into the Free State Health Department, including a new investigation by the Human Rights Commission who will be wrapping up its results soon, an investigation by the National Health ombudsman into five babies who died in one week at Bongani Hospital in Welkom in 2015 and the TAC and Section27's People's Commission of Inquiry last year where more than 60 people came to testify. The department of Health didn't bother to put their side of the story.

It is almost incomprehensible as to how different healthcare in the province is viewed by patients and doctors on the ground and the department - it is as if they are talking about different provinces.

Press Release:


Free State’s Haemorrhaging Healthcare
Last week Carte Blanche exposed a controversial stem cell unit at Pelonomi hospital. Despite having operated since June, last week the Medicines Control Council ordered the doctor running the unit to stop all treatments. Then the Department of Health in the province cancelled the controversial unit’s contract calling it a ’bad decision’ on their part. Over the past three years, Carte Blanche has uncovered widespread maladministration in the Free State’s public health sector. Little has changed...from a serious shortage of doctors, specialists and nurses to cases of medical negligence and the credibility of the University of the Free State Medical School hanging in the balance. Is the Free State’s healthcare system on the brink of collapse?


Script:


FS HEALTH 2016 COLLAPSE

PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK

PRESENTER: DEVI SANKAREE GOVERNDER

EDITOR: JAMES CARROLL

BROADCAST DATE: 9 OCTOBER 2016

BEN BARNARD: My boy was sent there to uncover this to show the people that that is how they treat babies and that is the respect that that hospital has for life.

BEAUTY MONYEGISA: Ja, ek is baie kwaad. As hulle help my hierso, miskien my baba was hierso by my hande.
(Yes, I’m very angry. If they’d helped me here, I could perhaps have been holding my baby now.)

BONGANI INSIDER: BONGANI DR: There are people who believe that we are not in crisis, but we are. It gets worse… people die.

For years now, the Free State Department of Health has faced an onslaught of negative publicity - on the brink of collapse, declared unfit to manage its budget and placed under administration.

Last Sunday, we exposed a controversial stem cell unit at Pelenomi Hospital in Bloemfontein – the Free State’s largest hospital. While we were investigating, the National Health Department stepped in, instructed the doctor running it to immediately stop treating patients and the Free State Health Department cancelled the contract and closed the unit.
On Monday this week, Free State Premier Ace Magashule reshuffled his cabinet and Health MEC, Dr Benny Malakoane was moved to another portfolio.

Calls for dr Malakoane’s head have been consistent since his appointment in 2013. But he has maintained throughout his tenure there was not crisis.

[CARTE BLANCHE: 28 MARCH 2015] DR BENNY MALAKOANE: The health system is not collapsing.

And Head of the Health Department, dr David Motau is optimistic.

DR DAVID MOTAU: There are challenges here and there, but we are managing those challenges.




But the patients they serve report a different reality.
Not only does the Free State currently have 23 doctors per 100 000 patients, but the province also has the second highest infant mortality rate in the country - 218 deaths per hundred thousand births.

DEVI LINK: Bongani Hospital made headlines in October last year when five babies died in a space of one week. The Health Ombudsman is investigating.

Baby Ethan Barnard’s parents are haunted by their ordeal at Bongani Hospital in Welkom.
Cindi Barnard went into labour 26 weeks into her pregnancy.

CINDI: die dokter het ‘n sonar kom doen, hy het toe vir my gesê die babatjie is te klein, hy gaan dit nie maak nie. Ek het toe gekraam in die wagarea – alleen – die suster het verdwyn. Toe sy terugkom, het sy hom net gevat en geloop en ek was onder die indruk sy vat hom NICU toe, want hy het gelewe.
(The doctor came to do a sonar and then told me that the baby was too small, he was not going to make it. I then gave birth in the waiting area – alone – the nurse disappeared. When she returned, she just took him away and left and I was under the impression that she was taking him to NICU, because he was alive.)

About three hours after Ethan’s birth, a nurse told Cindi that he died.

CINDI: Hulle het vir my ‘n papier gebring gebring en gesê hy is te klein begrawe te word, hy moet veras word, ek moet hierdie papier teken daarvoor. Ek het later eers uitgevind dis die papier wat sê hy kan maar saam met medical waste gebrand word.
(They brought me a form and said he was too small to be buried, he should be cremated and that I should sign the form for that purpose. I only found out later it was the form authorising him to be incinerated with medical waste.)

A Bongani insider confirmed Cindi’s version of the events.

BONGANI DR: When you take the baby from the mother, you don’t take the baby to the sluice room – explain to the family, based on what you have found, what is happening.

DEVI LINK: If a baby is born under 26 weeks without taking a single breath, then the body has to be disposed of as medical waste. But Baby Ethan was alive when he was taken away by a nurse – and when he was found by another nurse six hours later – he was still breathing.

BONGANI DR: I know that they said the baby was taken to the sluice room because they felt it was a miscarriage.

BEN: I was flabbergasted. I didn’t know what to do. I didn’t know what to feel. I just wanted to run and hold my boy…

Even after Ethan was rescued from the sluice room, he was still not put in an incubator immediately.

BEN: I asked him: “Doctor, My baby is in a crib, why is he in a crib?” He then told me: “The baby was born before, or under a 1000g and that a baby born under a 1000g is not priority to the hospital.”

Ben says this doctor quickly changed his story when he was told Ethan survived for six hours without any aid.
Baby Ethan developed jaundice and other complications and passed away two weeks after he was born.

BEN: And I stood with my boy and I told him: “I’m sorry and that I love him.”

The department didn’t want to comment and is investigating the case, so the cause of Baby Ethan’s death is not yet known.

But, has healthcare at the 700-bed Bongani Regional Hospital already imploded?

BONGANI DR: Currently there are 28 medical officers, we are supposed to have 45 medical officers.

The HPCSA confirmed that it cancelled the hospital’s accreditation to train interns effective 2017.

DR DAVID MOTAU: The issues were issues of specialists. It has been resolved as far as specialists are concerned. I have a full complement now as we speak.

But, the department’s own HR documents reflect that there are currently only four specialists at Bongani Hospital instead of the required seven. Even more contradictory is a list sent by Bongani’s acting CEO, stating that there are ten specialists – three more than the number approved by the department.

BONGANI DR: The two surgeons have resigned, so surgery is not operating anymore. We are left with junior medical officers – the most experienced is three years, they can’t even do basic skills. Anaesthesia doesn’t have a specialist, it is being run by medical officers.

Dr Freek Bester is the Free State President of the South African Medical Association and speaks on behalf of all state doctors in the province.

DR FREEK BESTER: It’s a practical crisis of delivering health care to people who are entitled to good proper health care.

REGISTRAR: Every year it’s just getting worse.

This Pelenomi senior registrar, who prefers and prefers not to be identified, says the Department of Health is out of touch.
REGISTRAR: We on the floor, that have to deal with the patients, see the disastrous ends.

Over the last three years, Carte Blanche has uncovered widespread maladministration in healthcare in the province. We found desperate and overworked doctors and nurses; a lack of basic medication and equipment.

DR BESTER: The doctors that they put there, which are not even always trained in SA context are not well skilled for instance to do caesarean sections or emergency surgical procedures.

REGISTRAR: Kroonstad and Welkom – don’t have doctors after hours, which means that many nights those patients get referred to us as well - that would include stab wounds, mothers in labour for very long.

This happened to 35-year old Beauty Monyegisa who went into labour 36 weeks into her pregnancy on Sunday, the 3rd of July.

BEAUTY: Die ambulans het my hierso by die huis kom vat, toe gaan ons daarso by die Sasolburg Hospitaal.
(The ambulance came to fetch me at my house and took me to Sasolburg Hospital.

Beauty needed an emergency caeseraen. From Sasolburg she was taken to Boitumelo Hospital in Kroonstad. But Beauty says the ambulance stopped several times along the way at petrol stations and toll gates and it took five hours to cover the 120km journey.

BEAUTY: Sy’s net een dokter. Toe sê sy: “O, God!” Toe se sy hulle moet my vinnig vat tot Bloemfontein.
(There was only one doctor. She said: “Oh, God!” Then she said they should quickly take me to Bloemfontein.)

A trip from Kroonstad to Bloemfontein should take two hours. Beauty only arrived at Universitas Hospital four hours later – and she says it’s unclear why it took twice as long. In theatre, it was discovered that her uterus had ruptured during the night and her baby died.
The final report said a caeserean should have been done at Boitumelo Hospital, but no doctors were on call. The department didn’t want to comment on the case.

BEAUTY: Dis die hospitaal se skuld.
(It’s the hospital’s fault.)

But even when hospitals have the equipment it cannot be fully utilised because of a lack of staff.
In 2008, Carte Blanche started its Making-A-Difference Campaign to raise funds to equip, refurbish and/or create Paediatric operating theatres, ICU and High Care Wards in state hospitals.
In 2009, our campaign donated 6,5 million rands worth of equipment to Universitas’ Paediatric ICU and High Care Wards.

But, in 2011 we discovered the High Care Ward was only open for two days after the official opening - and in August this year, we discovered that the ward was closed again due to a lack of nursing staff. Shortly after our inquiries, it was opened again. And our request to visit the ward, was declined.

DR DAVID MOTAU: Neonatal ICU, it’s a speciality. All that we did was to integrate the two, that’s it. The beds are still there.

DEVI: The right thing to do would be to go back to your donors and say: “Look, guys, we have a problem.”

DR DAVID MOTAU: It was wrong of us not to tell you, but we want to ask you to donate more.

DEVI: You want more donations, but when we wanted to go and have a look at our own ward that we equipped, the answer was no.

DR DAVID MOTAU: You are going to go in there and film.

DEVI: Yes

DR DAVID MOTAU: We cannot allow that to happen.

DEVI: Why?

DR DAVID MOTAU: Remember, these are patients, we have to respect…

DEVI: We don’t show patients’ faces, you know that.

DR DAVID MOTAU: No, no, we have to respect the rights of patients.

DEVI: So do we.

The University of the Free State’s Medical students are taught primarily at Universitas and also at Pelenomi hospitals.

DEVI LINK: We discovered that the future of specialised training at the School of Medicine at the University of the Free State was under threat. With the Health Professions Council of SA granting ONLY partial accreditation to four departments.

The HPCSA’s assessment was done in March this year – after more than a 170 doctors and specialists left between 2014 and ’15. The requirement was that more staff should be appointed in those departments.

DR FREEK BESTER: Since they got this conditional accreditation to give training to medical doctors, things have gone worse. We did not get more doctors on board.

This year, at least another 14 specialists left. Medical students are dissatisfied with their training.

DR FREEK BESTER: We should have 225 medical professionals. Currently they have got less than hundred doctors appointed and the big problem also is the super-specialists have all gone.

DR DAVID MOTAU: Currently we are busy with interviews and we have just appointed now the head of clinical department at Universitas for obs and gynae which was a problem. Anaesthesiology, we also appointing there.

REGISTRAR: According to HPCSA regulations we are supposed to be 1 consultant to 3 registrars. In Pelenomi specifically, there is only one consultant, whereas there are thirteen registrars. We don’t get the training, how can you teach medical students when you don’t know what you have to teach.

But the Medical School denies this claim. And the HPCSA told us it wasn’t aware of this situation.

REGISTRAR: When you want for instance take a patient to theatre, there is always a struggle. Either the anaesathetic machine is not working; in theatre the aircon is not working, your theatre list gets cancelled and then you end up with patients with wound sepsis; or there are not enough anaetheselogists.

DR DAVID MOTAU: Yes, a theatre list will be cancelled for various other reasons.

DEVI: Not because of lack of equipment?

DR DAVID MOTAU: Not….

DEVI: And doctors?

DR DAVID MOTAU: Lack of equipment can be one of the reasons, lack of doctors can be one of the reasons.

But possibly most shocking, is the registrar’s allegation that because theatre lists are cancelled so often, some registrars have problems reaching the required quota of surgical cases in order to qualify as specialists.

REGISTRAR: Part of our training requires you to fill in a log book to provide evidence that you have obtained the adequate skills to perform basic surgery. In the end the registrar who has to obtain these skills can’t do that, because they don’t get the chance to operate. So, if there is no one that can teach you or even make sure that you are an adequate surgeon before you leave, it is very easy to make these cases up and then in the end pass your exam.

DR DAVID MOTAU: That is not correct. They have platforms where they need to raise this.

On Monday, Butana Khompela replaced dr Benny Malakoane as the MEC for Health. Perhaps he will usher in sorely needed change.

BONGANI DR: The mother of the baby who died…talks to me, I see the tears .. you don't’ . I feel her pain, because I can see she is crying for her baby. Deep down I know something could have happened, but I cannot say so to her.


PROMO’S

PROMO 1:15

BONGANI INSIDER: There are people who believe that we are not in crisis, but we are. People die.
We go back to the Free State where patients’ reality of public healthcare is completely different from the department that runs it.
BEN: And I stood with my boy and I told him: “I’m sorry and that I love him.”

PROMO 2: 15”

BEN BARNARD: My boy was sent there to uncover this to show the people that that is how they treat babies.
Is the Free State’s public healthcare system on the brink of collapse? We return to see if anything has improved.

PROMO 3:10”

BEAUTY: Ek is baie kwaad. Dis die hospitaal se skuld.

What’s crippling the Free State’s public healthcare system?

Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 05 December 2016 09 October 2016 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 01 November 2016 Press Release: Free State’s Haemorrhaging Healthcare Last week Carte Blanche exposed a controversial stem cell unit at Pelonomi hospital. Despite having operated since June, last week the Medicines Control Council ordered the doctor running the unit to stop all treatments. Then the Department of Health in the province cancelled the controversial unit’s contract calling it a ’bad decision’ on their part. Over the past three years, Carte Blanche has uncovered widespread maladministration in the Free State’s public health sector. Little has changed...from a serious shortage of doctors, specialists and nurses to cases of medical negligence and the credibility of the University of the Free State Medical School hanging in the balance. Is the Free State’s healthcare system on the brink of collapse? Script: FS HEALTH 2016 COLLAPSE PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK PRESENTER: DEVI SANKAREE GOVERNDER EDITOR: JAMES CARROLL BROADCAST DATE: 9 OCTOBER 2016 BEN BARNARD: My boy was sent there to uncover this to show the people that that is how they treat babies and that is the respect that that hospital has for life. BEAUTY MONYEGISA: Ja, ek is baie kwaad. As hulle help my hierso, miskien my baba was hierso by my hande. (Yes, I’m very angry. If they’d helped me here, I could perhaps have been holding my baby now.) BONGANI INSIDER: BONGANI DR: There are people who believe that we are not in crisis, but we are. It gets worse… people die. For years now, the Free State Department of Health has faced an onslaught of negative publicity - on the brink of collapse, declared unfit to manage its budget and placed under administration. Last Sunday, we exposed a controversial stem cell unit at Pelenomi Hospital in Bloemfontein – the Free State’s largest hospital. While we were investigating, the National Health Department stepped in, instructed the doctor running it to immediately stop treating patients and the Free State Health Department cancelled the contract and closed the unit. On Monday this week, Free State Premier Ace Magashule reshuffled his cabinet and Health MEC, Dr Benny Malakoane was moved to another portfolio. Calls for dr Malakoane’s head have been consistent since his appointment in 2013. But he has maintained throughout his tenure there was not crisis. [CARTE BLANCHE: 28 MARCH 2015] DR BENNY MALAKOANE: The health system is not collapsing. And Head of the Health Department, dr David Motau is optimistic. DR DAVID MOTAU: There are challenges here and there, but we are managing those challenges. But the patients they serve report a different reality. Not only does the Free State currently have 23 doctors per 100 000 patients, but the province also has the second highest infant mortality rate in the country - 218 deaths per hundred thousand births. DEVI LINK: Bongani Hospital made headlines in October last year when five babies died in a space of one week. The Health Ombudsman is investigating. Baby Ethan Barnard’s parents are haunted by their ordeal at Bongani Hospital in Welkom. Cindi Barnard went into labour 26 weeks into her pregnancy. CINDI: die dokter het ‘n sonar kom doen, hy het toe vir my gesê die babatjie is te klein, hy gaan dit nie maak nie. Ek het toe gekraam in die wagarea – alleen – die suster het verdwyn. Toe sy terugkom, het sy hom net gevat en geloop en ek was onder die indruk sy vat hom NICU toe, want hy het gelewe. (The doctor came to do a sonar and then told me that the baby was too small, he was not going to make it. I then gave birth in the waiting area – alone – the nurse disappeared. When she returned, she just took him away and left and I was under the impression that she was taking him to NICU, because he was alive.) About three hours after Ethan’s birth, a nurse told Cindi that he died. CINDI: Hulle het vir my ‘n papier gebring gebring en gesê hy is te klein begrawe te word, hy moet veras word, ek moet hierdie papier teken daarvoor. Ek het later eers uitgevind dis die papier wat sê hy kan maar saam met medical waste gebrand word. (They brought me a form and said he was too small to be buried, he should be cremated and that I should sign the form for that purpose. I only found out later it was the form authorising him to be incinerated with medical waste.) A Bongani insider confirmed Cindi’s version of the events. BONGANI DR: When you take the baby from the mother, you don’t take the baby to the sluice room – explain to the family, based on what you have found, what is happening. DEVI LINK: If a baby is born under 26 weeks without taking a single breath, then the body has to be disposed of as medical waste. But Baby Ethan was alive when he was taken away by a nurse – and when he was found by another nurse six hours later – he was still breathing. BONGANI DR: I know that they said the baby was taken to the sluice room because they felt it was a miscarriage. BEN: I was flabbergasted. I didn’t know what to do. I didn’t know what to feel. I just wanted to run and hold my boy… Even after Ethan was rescued from the sluice room, he was still not put in an incubator immediately. BEN: I asked him: “Doctor, My baby is in a crib, why is he in a crib?” He then told me: “The baby was born before, or under a 1000g and that a baby born under a 1000g is not priority to the hospital.” Ben says this doctor quickly changed his story when he was told Ethan survived for six hours without any aid. Baby Ethan developed jaundice and other complications and passed away two weeks after he was born. BEN: And I stood with my boy and I told him: “I’m sorry and that I love him.” The department didn’t want to comment and is investigating the case, so the cause of Baby Ethan’s death is not yet known. But, has healthcare at the 700-bed Bongani Regional Hospital already imploded? BONGANI DR: Currently there are 28 medical officers, we are supposed to have 45 medical officers. The HPCSA confirmed that it cancelled the hospital’s accreditation to train interns effective 2017. DR DAVID MOTAU: The issues were issues of specialists. It has been resolved as far as specialists are concerned. I have a full complement now as we speak. But, the department’s own HR documents reflect that there are currently only four specialists at Bongani Hospital instead of the required seven. Even more contradictory is a list sent by Bongani’s acting CEO, stating that there are ten specialists – three more than the number approved by the department. BONGANI DR: The two surgeons have resigned, so surgery is not operating anymore. We are left with junior medical officers – the most experienced is three years, they can’t even do basic skills. Anaesthesia doesn’t have a specialist, it is being run by medical officers. Dr Freek Bester is the Free State President of the South African Medical Association and speaks on behalf of all state doctors in the province. DR FREEK BESTER: It’s a practical crisis of delivering health care to people who are entitled to good proper health care. REGISTRAR: Every year it’s just getting worse. This Pelenomi senior registrar, who prefers and prefers not to be identified, says the Department of Health is out of touch. REGISTRAR: We on the floor, that have to deal with the patients, see the disastrous ends. Over the last three years, Carte Blanche has uncovered widespread maladministration in healthcare in the province. We found desperate and overworked doctors and nurses; a lack of basic medication and equipment. DR BESTER: The doctors that they put there, which are not even always trained in SA context are not well skilled for instance to do caesarean sections or emergency surgical procedures. REGISTRAR: Kroonstad and Welkom – don’t have doctors after hours, which means that many nights those patients get referred to us as well - that would include stab wounds, mothers in labour for very long. This happened to 35-year old Beauty Monyegisa who went into labour 36 weeks into her pregnancy on Sunday, the 3rd of July. BEAUTY: Die ambulans het my hierso by die huis kom vat, toe gaan ons daarso by die Sasolburg Hospitaal. (The ambulance came to fetch me at my house and took me to Sasolburg Hospital. Beauty needed an emergency caeseraen. From Sasolburg she was taken to Boitumelo Hospital in Kroonstad. But Beauty says the ambulance stopped several times along the way at petrol stations and toll gates and it took five hours to cover the 120km journey. BEAUTY: Sy’s net een dokter. Toe sê sy: “O, God!” Toe se sy hulle moet my vinnig vat tot Bloemfontein. (There was only one doctor. She said: “Oh, God!” Then she said they should quickly take me to Bloemfontein.) A trip from Kroonstad to Bloemfontein should take two hours. Beauty only arrived at Universitas Hospital four hours later – and she says it’s unclear why it took twice as long. In theatre, it was discovered that her uterus had ruptured during the night and her baby died. The final report said a caeserean should have been done at Boitumelo Hospital, but no doctors were on call. The department didn’t want to comment on the case. BEAUTY: Dis die hospitaal se skuld. (It’s the hospital’s fault.) But even when hospitals have the equipment it cannot be fully utilised because of a lack of staff. In 2008, Carte Blanche started its Making-A-Difference Campaign to raise funds to equip, refurbish and/or create Paediatric operating theatres, ICU and High Care Wards in state hospitals. In 2009, our campaign donated 6,5 million rands worth of equipment to Universitas’ Paediatric ICU and High Care Wards. But, in 2011 we discovered the High Care Ward was only open for two days after the official opening - and in August this year, we discovered that the ward was closed again due to a lack of nursing staff. Shortly after our inquiries, it was opened again. And our request to visit the ward, was declined. DR DAVID MOTAU: Neonatal ICU, it’s a speciality. All that we did was to integrate the two, that’s it. The beds are still there. DEVI: The right thing to do would be to go back to your donors and say: “Look, guys, we have a problem.” DR DAVID MOTAU: It was wrong of us not to tell you, but we want to ask you to donate more. DEVI: You want more donations, but when we wanted to go and have a look at our own ward that we equipped, the answer was no. DR DAVID MOTAU: You are going to go in there and film. DEVI: Yes DR DAVID MOTAU: We cannot allow that to happen. DEVI: Why? DR DAVID MOTAU: Remember, these are patients, we have to respect… DEVI: We don’t show patients’ faces, you know that. DR DAVID MOTAU: No, no, we have to respect the rights of patients. DEVI: So do we. The University of the Free State’s Medical students are taught primarily at Universitas and also at Pelenomi hospitals. DEVI LINK: We discovered that the future of specialised training at the School of Medicine at the University of the Free State was under threat. With the Health Professions Council of SA granting ONLY partial accreditation to four departments. The HPCSA’s assessment was done in March this year – after more than a 170 doctors and specialists left between 2014 and ’15. The requirement was that more staff should be appointed in those departments. DR FREEK BESTER: Since they got this conditional accreditation to give training to medical doctors, things have gone worse. We did not get more doctors on board. This year, at least another 14 specialists left. Medical students are dissatisfied with their training. DR FREEK BESTER: We should have 225 medical professionals. Currently they have got less than hundred doctors appointed and the big problem also is the super-specialists have all gone. DR DAVID MOTAU: Currently we are busy with interviews and we have just appointed now the head of clinical department at Universitas for obs and gynae which was a problem. Anaesthesiology, we also appointing there. REGISTRAR: According to HPCSA regulations we are supposed to be 1 consultant to 3 registrars. In Pelenomi specifically, there is only one consultant, whereas there are thirteen registrars. We don’t get the training, how can you teach medical students when you don’t know what you have to teach. But the Medical School denies this claim. And the HPCSA told us it wasn’t aware of this situation. REGISTRAR: When you want for instance take a patient to theatre, there is always a struggle. Either the anaesathetic machine is not working; in theatre the aircon is not working, your theatre list gets cancelled and then you end up with patients with wound sepsis; or there are not enough anaetheselogists. DR DAVID MOTAU: Yes, a theatre list will be cancelled for various other reasons. DEVI: Not because of lack of equipment? DR DAVID MOTAU: Not…. DEVI: And doctors? DR DAVID MOTAU: Lack of equipment can be one of the reasons, lack of doctors can be one of the reasons. But possibly most shocking, is the registrar’s allegation that because theatre lists are cancelled so often, some registrars have problems reaching the required quota of surgical cases in order to qualify as specialists. REGISTRAR: Part of our training requires you to fill in a log book to provide evidence that you have obtained the adequate skills to perform basic surgery. In the end the registrar who has to obtain these skills can’t do that, because they don’t get the chance to operate. So, if there is no one that can teach you or even make sure that you are an adequate surgeon before you leave, it is very easy to make these cases up and then in the end pass your exam. DR DAVID MOTAU: That is not correct. They have platforms where they need to raise this. On Monday, Butana Khompela replaced dr Benny Malakoane as the MEC for Health. Perhaps he will usher in sorely needed change. BONGANI DR: The mother of the baby who died…talks to me, I see the tears .. you don't’ . I feel her pain, because I can see she is crying for her baby. Deep down I know something could have happened, but I cannot say so to her. PROMO’S PROMO 1:15 BONGANI INSIDER: There are people who believe that we are not in crisis, but we are. People die. We go back to the Free State where patients’ reality of public healthcare is completely different from the department that runs it. BEN: And I stood with my boy and I told him: “I’m sorry and that I love him.” PROMO 2: 15” BEN BARNARD: My boy was sent there to uncover this to show the people that that is how they treat babies. Is the Free State’s public healthcare system on the brink of collapse? We return to see if anything has improved. PROMO 3:10” BEAUTY: Ek is baie kwaad. Dis die hospitaal se skuld. What’s crippling the Free State’s public healthcare system?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Carte Blanche have been uncovering widespread maladministration in healthcare in the FS for the past three years. We go back to see if anything has changed.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The Free State Health department has been cash-strapped and under administration from the provincial legislature since 2014. They've had a debt of R700 million when they started the financial year in 2015/2016 - a debt, the department now says they have decreased to R200 million. A save of R500 million in just two financial years? Coupled with this, 24% of the province's doctors have resigned between 2014 - 2015, with another 14 specialists leaving in 2016. This has put the School of Medicine at the University of the Free State at great risk in terms of its accreditation and students - undergraduate and post-graduate are saying that they are not getting adequate training. Bongani Hospital in Welkom has lost its accreditation from the HPCSA this year and from the 1st of January 2017 the hospital will not be allowed to train and teach interns anymore.
metadata.Summary: Our source at Bongani Hospital also claims that by the end of October there will only be one specialists left, and by the end of December only one. However, the department is denying this, saying Bongani Hospital has a full spectrum of specialists and the hospital is able to provide all the necessary health services. The HOD of the FS department, dr David Motau, further says that healthcare in the province is at a healthy state and that they are improving. But this is not what doctors on the ground experience - doctors and nurses who have spoken to us in hidden identity. It is also not what human rights organisations, Section27 and the TAC are experiencing when they talk to medical practitioners on the ground. Just last week there were strikes at the Monapo Hospital in Qwaqwa again.
metadata.Further information: Our case studies tell horrendous stories of alleged medical malpractice that resulted in them losing their babies. The Carte Blanche Paediatric High Care Ward at Universitas Hospital has been closed for the month of August - confirmed by the head of Paediatrics, but then denied by the HOD. We also asked him why, if it is in fact our ward, the department didn't want to give us permission to go and film there. The HOD said because we will film footage in a hospital and we are not allowed to, but that the department wants to ask Carte Blanche to please donate more equipment to the hospitals in the Free State. The Minister of Health says the National Department is concerned about what is going on in the Free State province's healthcare. But the Minister admitted that he cannot hire of fire any MEC for Health. He doesn't have the authority to do so. Only the Premier of a province can do that. So, is change in the Free State healthcare really possible with a MEC for health and a HOD for health who both say healthcare in the province is not bad and in a healthy state? There have been consistent calls for MEC, dr Benny Malakoane's head for years. There are several investigations into the Free State Health Department, including a new investigation by the Human Rights Commission who will be wrapping up its results soon, an investigation by the National Health ombudsman into five babies who died in one week at Bongani Hospital in Welkom in 2015 and the TAC and Section27's People's Commission of Inquiry last year where more than 60 people came to testify. The department of Health didn't bother to put their side of the story. It is almost incomprehensible as to how different healthcare in the province is viewed by patients and doctors on the ground and the department - it is as if they are talking about different provinces.
